proclivity

/proh-KLIV-ih-tee/ - the stress falls on KLIV · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Proclivity means a natural tendency or inclination toward something.

The kitten's proclivity for high places announced itself the day she was found asleep on top of the refrigerator.

Example

Every roommate quiz asked the same question in different words, and Dana answered honestly: given a free Saturday, she would reorganize something - the spice rack, the closet, the garage. A proclivity for imposing order, the survey called it, and it had been visible since her crayon days, when she sorted the box by warmth of color.

Proclivity is more specific than habit or preference: it names a natural leaning - the built-in tilt of a personality toward one kind of thing. Habits are acquired and can be broken; a proclivity was there before you noticed it, pulling like a slope.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tendency: A tendency is any leaning at all, in people or in things — even clouds and markets have tendencies. Proclivity belongs to persons: a natural, built-in tilt of the personality toward one kind of thing, there before you ever noticed it.

predisposition: A predisposition is a built-in readiness for something to develop, said as often of health as of character — a predisposition to colds or to worry. Proclivity is about conduct: the natural leaning that shows in what a person repeatedly chooses and does.

penchant: A penchant is a strong liking — a taste you happily indulge, for loud ties or midnight snacks. Proclivity runs deeper than taste: a built-in tilt of the whole personality toward one kind of thing, showing in conduct since childhood, not just in what pleases you.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

distaste: an active dislike

reluctance: a holding back from the thing

Where it sits · how strong the pull toward it is

leaning → proclivity → compulsion

leaning vs. proclivity: A leaning is a gentle pull you can ignore; a proclivity tilts the whole personality toward the thing, visibly and repeatedly.

compulsion vs. proclivity: Compulsion goes beyond proclivity: a proclivity inclines you toward what you would choose anyway, while compulsion drives you whether you choose it or not.

Which word fits?

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pro-: forward

Root — cliv-: slope (Latin clivus)

Suffix — -ity: state of being

Put it together: Pro- (forward) + cliv- (Latin clivus, 'slope') + -ity (the state of being) = the state of sloping forward. A proclivity is a built-in downhill grade: left to itself, the personality rolls that way. Latin clivus survives in no common English word, though its ancient cousin gives us incline and lean - the very picture proclivity paints.

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin clivus, 'slope,' never took root in English on its own - its other descendants, acclivity and declivity, are rare surveyors' terms. Distant cousins from the same ancient 'lean' root did thrive: incline, and even lean itself. Proclivity keeps the old slope frozen inside it.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Proclivity is slightly formal and pairs with 'for': a proclivity for order, for risk, for high places. Say tendency in everyday talk. Choose proclivity when you mean a leaning that feels built into the person rather than picked up along the way.
